publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Task difficulty and performance induce diverse adaptive patterns in gain and shape of primary auditory cortical receptive fields

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: rapid changes in A1 spectrotemporal receptive fields while an animal detects a tone in noise
span.quote: This study explored the neural correlates of this perceptual ability by measuring rapid changes of spectrotemporal receptive fields (STRFs) in primary auditory cortex during detection of a target tone embedded in noise.

span.label: whether the magnitude of task-driven receptive field plasticity depends on task difficulty, and whether the change is one of gain or of shape
span.quote: However, an important and currently unresolved question is whether the magnitude of these changes is influenced by task difficulty, or more specifically, by the perceptual difference between the target and reference signals that the animal must discriminate. Furthermore, it is unknown how exactly the underlying receptive fields change under these circumstances, i.e., whether they simply exhibit a modulated gain, or alternatively, a change of shape such as tuning or bandwidth.

span.label: separates gain from shape change and shows they move in opposite directions, with the sign of the net effect set jointly by task difficulty and by the cell's distance from the target frequency
span.quote: Compared to responses in the passive state, STRF gain decreased during task performance in most cells. By contrast, STRF shape changes were excitatory and specific, being strongest in cells with best frequencies near the target tone.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: The net effect of these adaptations was to accentuate the representation of the target tone relative to the noise, by enhancing responses of near -target cells to the tone during high-SNR tasks, while suppressing responses of far -from-target cells to the masking noise in low-SNR tasks.

span.label: rapid task-related plasticity of auditory cortical receptive fields
span.quote: We have previously described a form of rapid cortical plasticity in which the spectro-temporal receptive fields (STRFs) in primary auditory cortex (A1) adapt during the task in a manner that maximizes the discrimination of the target (foreground) relative to reference (background) signals ( Fritz et al., 2003 ).

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: This study explored the neural correlates of this perceptual ability by measuring rapid changes of spectrotemporal receptive fields (STRFs) in primary auditory cortex during detection of a target tone embedded in noise.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Lowering target SNR raises the attentional effort the animal must invest, and that increased effort drives larger adaptive changes in the receptive field
span.quote: As target SNR decreased, distinguishing the target from the reference noise became more difficult, requiring more attention or effort, which, we predicted, could cause larger adaptive changes in the STRF.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Pulling a tone out of a masker requires simultaneously suppressing the responses driven by the concurrent noise and enhancing sensitivity to the tone
span.quote: Hence the process of extracting the tone component of the target necessitated suppression of responses to this concurrent masking noise while simultaneously enhancing the sensitivity to the target tone.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Which direction a cell changes is set by what drives it: near cells are enhanced by proximity to the target tone, far cells are suppressed because the behaviourally relevant broadband masker drives them
span.quote: In the current experiments, the excitatory enhancements induced in the near-cells stem from their proximity to the target tone, whereas the strong suppression in the far cells was due to the behaviorally relevant broadband masking noise that surrounded the target and drove the responses in those cells.

span.label: a contrast matched filter: the acoustic features of the foreground are enhanced and those of the background suppressed
span.quote: In all these experiments, the pattern of STRF changes that emerged followed a simple model in which the acoustic features of the foreground were enhanced and those of the background suppressed, a hypothesis which we called a “contrast matched filter

span.label: the net effect keeps the target salient by two different routes - enhancing near cells when the tone is loud, suppressing far cells when it is buried
span.quote: To summarize, in high SNR tasks, the target induces positive changes in nearby STRFs, thereby enhancing the representation of the target tone, similar to earlier findings with pure-tone targets ( Fritz et al., 2003 ). Decreasing the target tone (low SNR) causes overall gain suppression, especially in far cells, thereby maintaining the enhanced representation of the target tone responses relative to those of the masking noise.

span.label: the active STRF is modelled explicitly as a scaled passive STRF plus an orthogonal shape change, S_d = g.S_b + delta
span.quote: We defined the active (during) STRF ( S d ) as the sum of a scaled passive (before-task) STRF ( S b ) and a change in the shape of the STRF, i.e.: S d = g ․ S b + δ, where g is the gain that reflects the fraction of the STRF that maintained its original shape, and δ is the remaining (orthogonal) shape change that could not be captured by scaling S b (this δ was used to generate the plots in Fig.7C ).

span.label: STRFs are measured from the reference TORCs alone, never during target presentation, so the measurement does not include the target
span.quote: The key feature of the tone-in-noise task is that, unlike the case with pure-tone targets, the TORCs appeared not only as reference stimuli but also as maskers in the target stimulus, thus reducing the perceptual difference between target and reference signals.

span.label: attentional load is validated behaviourally by inserting identical intermediate-difficulty probes into easy and hard blocks
span.quote: To test the hypothesis that more attentional resources were devoted during difficult (low SNR) tasks than during easy (high SNR) tasks, we modified the task structure by randomly inserting probe trials (25%) of intermediate difficulty during a block of difficult or easy trials (75%). We reasoned that if detection levels of the rarer probes reflected the overall attentional level of the animal during the task that increased with task difficulty, then performance on the probe trials should be better during difficult tasks than during easy tasks

span.label: STRF frequency resolution is too coarse to exclude that some A1 neurons build narrow matched filters at the exact target frequency.
span.quote: However, because of the limited frequency resolution of our STRFs, we also cannot rule out the possibility that some A1 neurons adaptively reshape their receptive fields to create narrow, highly selective, spectral matched filters for the target tone frequency.

span.label: It is unknown how far the gain-reduction/shape-enhancement pattern is specific to the tone-in-noise task, its avoidance paradigm, or the fixed noise level.
span.quote: It is unclear to what extent this pattern of broad gain reduction and focused shape enhancement was dependent on the specifics of the tone-in-noise task.

span.label: Most cells could not be held across multiple task conditions, so difficulty comparisons are largely between rather than within cells.
span.quote: Ferrets performed two or three tasks in a given recording session, but it was not always possible to maintain recordings from the same cell throughout multiple task conditions.

span.label: Disentangling stimulus structure from behavioural paradigm requires further experiments; the interpretations offered are conjectures.
span.quote: While definitive resolution to these issues will require further experiments that dissociate the contributions of the stimulus structure and the behavioral paradigm to these changes, we nevertheless offer a few conjectures below based on what we already know from the results of previous studies of attention-driven effects in the auditory and visual systems.

span.label: The 0.6-octave boundary dividing near from far cells was an arbitrary choice.
span.quote: Apart from giving a roughly balanced population of each type (112 versus 125), the precise choice of this dividing line was arbitrary, and none of the results described below depended critically on its exact position (See Fig SD-4 in supplementary data ).

span.label: the near/far dividing line is arbitrary, stated as such, and shown not to change the results
span.quote: Cells were labeled as near the target if the unit’s BF was within 0.6 octaves from the target tone and as far otherwise. Apart from giving a roughly balanced population of each type (112 versus 125), the precise choice of this dividing line was arbitrary, and none of the results described below depended critically on its exact position

span.label: the standard STRF power normalisation used in the group's previous papers does not separate gain from shape
span.quote: As explained earlier, STRF power normalization , which we have used in previous publications ( Fritz et al., 2003 ; Fritz et al., 2005 ), does not completely differentiate between gain and shape changes.

span.label: the dependence of gain on task difficulty was NOT confirmed when all performance levels were pooled
span.quote: This weak dependence of the gain on task difficulty, however, was not confirmed when we pooled the results from all cells in this study, i.e., including all performance levels (see Figure SD-3A in Supplementary Data . where gain distributions remain relatively unchanged with SNR with medians of about 0.7).

span.label: changes often persisted after the task with no systematic relation to the type of plasticity
span.quote: Although we frequently observed persistent changes, there was no systematic trend in persistence versus the type of STRF plasticity.

span.label: most cells were recorded in only one task condition, so within-cell comparison across difficulties is limited
span.quote: Data were also subdivided into three groups according to the difficulty of the tasks, as parameterized by the target SNR. The three non-overlapping ranges were: high SNR (>=0 dB), mid SNR (0 dB > SNR >= −5 dB), low SNR (< −5 dB), with 93, 57, and 87 single-units in each range, respectively.

span.label: the finding that harder tasks recruit more attention, and the probe-trial design used to demonstrate it
span.quote: To test the hypothesis that more attentional resources were devoted during difficult (low SNR) tasks than during easy (high SNR) tasks, we modified the task structure by randomly inserting probe trials (25%) of intermediate difficulty during a block of difficult or easy trials (75%). We reasoned that if detection levels of the rarer probes reflected the overall attentional level of the animal during the task that increased with task difficulty, then performance on the probe trials should be better during difficult tasks than during easy tasks

span.label: the matched filter, imported as the model for how a receptive field should adapt to separate foreground from background
span.quote: In all these experiments, the pattern of STRF changes that emerged followed a simple model in which the acoustic features of the foreground were enhanced and those of the background suppressed, a hypothesis which we called a “contrast matched filter

span.label: plasticity here is rapid and reversible - measured as the difference between active and passive STRFs within a session, not as learning
span.quote: This study explored the neural correlates of this perceptual ability by measuring rapid changes of spectrotemporal receptive fields (STRFs) in primary auditory cortex during detection of a target tone embedded in noise.

span.label: task difficulty is operationalised as target SNR, and validated separately by lick withdrawal time and by probe-trial performance
span.quote: In order to develop a quantitative behavioral index of task difficulty, we measured the average lick withdrawal time (LWT) of the animal, which we defined to be the time after target onset when the animal to decreased its lick rate to half its average lick rate during the reference stimuli (i.e., down to 40% from 80% in Figure 2A ).

span.label: gain and shape are given distinct definitions by an explicit model: gain is the fraction of the STRF that keeps its original shape, shape change is the orthogonal remainder
span.quote: We defined the active (during) STRF ( S d ) as the sum of a scaled passive (before-task) STRF ( S b ) and a change in the shape of the STRF, i.e.: S d = g ․ S b + δ, where g is the gain that reflects the fraction of the STRF that maintained its original shape, and δ is the remaining (orthogonal) shape change that could not be captured by scaling S b (this δ was used to generate the plots in Fig.7C ).

span.label: near and far are defined by a 0.6-octave cut from the target frequency, which the paper calls arbitrary and tests
span.quote: Cells were labeled as near the target if the unit’s BF was within 0.6 octaves from the target tone and as far otherwise. Apart from giving a roughly balanced population of each type (112 versus 125), the precise choice of this dividing line was arbitrary, and none of the results described below depended critically on its exact position

span.label: extends → Fritz et al. (2003; 2005; 2007a,b), the group's earlier demonstrations of rapid task-related STRF plasticity with pure-tone targets
span.quote: This study extends those findings by examining the effects of modulating the difficulty of a tone detection task by embedding it in noise at different SNRs.

span.label: builds-on → the "contrast matched filter" hypothesis of Fritz et al. (2007a)
span.quote: In all these experiments, the pattern of STRF changes that emerged followed a simple model in which the acoustic features of the foreground were enhanced and those of the background suppressed, a hypothesis which we called a “contrast matched filter” ( Fritz et al., 2007a ).

span.label: extends → visual studies of task difficulty and attention (Boudreau et al., 2006; Spitzer et al., 1988; Spitzer and Richmond, 1991), which did not separate gain from shape
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS GAIN AGAINST SHAPE. 'THESE MEASUREMENTS, HOWEVER, DID NOT DISTINGUISH RECEPTIVE FIELD GAIN FROM SHAPE CHANGES, AND HOW INCREASED TASK DIFFICULTY AFFECTED THEM DIFFERENTIALLY.' Two ways a receptive field can change that a single measure cannot separate - so the earlier result is a sum of two effects that this paper's [7] then shows move differently with difficulty. Q-511.
span.quote: These measurements, however, did not distinguish receptive field gain from shape changes, and how increased task difficulty affected them differentially.

span.label: replicates → earlier task-related plasticity results from the same group in tone-versus-TORC and tone-versus-tone paradigms (Fritz et al., 2003; 2005; 2007b)
span.quote: The diverse pattern of STRF changes described in this report is broadly consistent with the types of plasticity observed in previous studies in which ferrets detected target tone(s) relative to a reference TORC noise ( Fritz et al., 2003 ; Fritz et al., 2007b ), or discriminated a target tone relative to a reference tone of a different frequency ( Fritz et al., 2005 ).

span.label: extends → Fritz et al. on rapid STRF plasticity with pure-tone targets
span.quote: In the current experiments, the observed pattern of plasticity was roughly similar when the target tone level was high relative to the noise (SNR >= 0 dB) and the BF of the cell

span.label: qualifies → the contrast matched filter model, by showing the sign of the change depends on difficulty and on distance from target
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS DISTANCE FROM THE TARGET FREQUENCY, AND THE SIGN FLIPS ACROSS IT. 'when we grouped the plasticity changes by near and far cells, it became apparent that NEAR CELLS ON AVERAGE WERE ENHANCED (red) WHEREAS FAR CELLS WERE SUPPRESSED (blue).' The matched-filter model is qualified rather than refuted: it holds, with a sign that depends on where the cell sits. Q-442.
span.quote: However, when we grouped the plasticity changes by near and far cells, it became apparent that near cells on average were enhanced (red) whereas far cells were suppressed (blue).

span.label: extends → visual studies showing task difficulty enhances attentional modulation, which did not separate gain from shape
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS GAIN AGAINST SHAPE, on a second target. Same sentence as [2]: 'THESE MEASUREMENTS DID NOT DISTINGUISH RECEPTIVE FIELD GAIN FROM SHAPE CHANGES.' One limitation of one earlier method, disqualifying it for two different claims this paper makes - which is why the sentence supports two rows rather than one. Q-511.
span.quote: These measurements, however, did not distinguish receptive field gain from shape changes, and how increased task difficulty affected them differentially.

span.label: qualifies → their own gain-versus-difficulty result, which did not survive pooling across performance levels
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHETHER THE CELLS ARE POOLED ACROSS PERFORMANCE LEVELS. 'THIS WEAK DEPENDENCE OF THE GAIN ON TASK DIFFICULTY, HOWEVER, WAS NOT CONFIRMED WHEN WE POOLED THE RESULTS FROM ALL CELLS IN THIS STUDY, I.E., INCLUDING ALL PERFORMANCE LEVELS.' The paper's own effect survives one analysis choice and not another, and it says which - an analyst decision reported as a result rather than buried in methods. Q-503.
span.quote: This weak dependence of the gain on task difficulty, however, was not confirmed when we pooled the results from all cells in this study, i.e., including all performance levels (see Figure SD-3A in Supplementary Data . where gain distributions remain relatively unchanged with SNR with medians of about 0.7).

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · task difficulty —operationalised-as→ signal-to-noise ratio
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span named neither endpoint; this clause states the operationalisation outright - difficulty IS the signal-to-noise ratio in this design. — strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: As target SNR decreased, distinguishing the target from the reference noise became more difficult, requiring more attention or effort, which, we predicted, could cause larger adaptive changes in the STRF.

span.label: gain —contrasted-with→ shape
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — the paper's central result: they move in OPPOSITE directions in the same cells - gain decreased while shape changes were excitatory
span.quote: Compared to responses in the passive state, STRF gain decreased during task performance in most cells. By contrast, STRF shape changes were excitatory and specific, being strongest in cells with best frequencies near the target tone.

span.label: task difficulty —causes→ attention
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — and it is tested rather than assumed, via probe trials of identical difficulty in easy and hard blocks
span.quote: To test the hypothesis that more attentional resources were devoted during difficult (low SNR) tasks than during easy (high SNR) tasks, we modified the task structure by randomly inserting probe trials (25%) of intermediate difficulty during a block of difficult or easy trials (75%). We reasoned that if detection levels of the rarer probes reflected the overall attentional level of the animal during the task that increased with task difficulty, then performance on the probe trials should be better during difficult tasks than during easy tasks

span.label: attention —operationalised-as→ probe trials
span.quote: To test the hypothesis that more attentional resources were devoted during difficult (low SNR) tasks than during easy (high SNR) tasks, we modified the task structure by randomly inserting probe trials (25%) of intermediate difficulty during a block of difficult or easy trials (75%). We reasoned that if detection levels of the rarer probes reflected the overall attentional level of the animal during the task that increased with task difficulty, then performance on the probe trials should be better during difficult tasks than during easy tasks

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · STRF —operationalised-as→ TORCs
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span named only the task design. This sentence names both and states the measurement outright - TORCs 'were used to MEASURE the STRF of the cell', which is exactly what `operationalised-as` records. — strength of the relation: 0.95 — the reference sounds are simultaneously the stimulus set and the measurement probe
span.quote: The key feature of the tone-in-noise task is that, unlike the case with pure-tone targets, the TORCs appeared not only as reference stimuli but also as maskers in the target stimulus, thus reducing the perceptual difference between target and reference signals.

span.label: task difficulty —operationalised-as→ signal-to-noise ratio
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — RE-GROUNDS Atiani2009-task-difficulty-and-performance-induce-diver[0]: the relation was always stated, the endpoint names were not in the span.
span.quote: task difficulty was modulated by varying the signal-to-noise ratio

span.label: STRF —operationalised-as→ TORCs
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — RE-GROUNDS Atiani2009-task-difficulty-and-performance-induce-diver[4]: the old span named ONE endpoint.
span.quote: In such a paradigm, the reference broadband noise was one of a set of 30 specially designed spectrotemporally modulated broadband noisy sounds - called TORCs - that were used to measure the STRF of the cell while the animal performed the task ( Klein et al., 2000 ).

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Using ANOVA we found that Δ BF changes for high and low SNR conditions were significantly different (p<0.05).

span.label: p-value
span.quote: Δ BF changes for high and low SNR conditions here were more distinctly different as demonstrated by the divergence in their means (p<0.01).

span.label: median
span.quote: In a majority of cells (> 66% in high SNR and near STRFs, and >80% in low SNR and far cells), the gain was <= 1 (median of approximately 0.9 and 0.7, respectively) indicating an overall suppression of the gain during behavior.

span.label: mean
span.quote: Suppression was weak in high and mid SNR tasks, and became significant (mean = −13.1 %; p < 0.05) only in the low SNR tasks.

span.label: ANOVA across SNR conditions
span.quote: Suppression was weak in high and mid SNR tasks, and became significant (mean = −13.1 %; p < 0.05) only in the low SNR tasks.

span.label: STRF power normalisation
span.quote: As explained earlier, STRF power normalization , which we have used in previous publications ( Fritz et al., 2003 ; Fritz et al., 2005 ), does not completely differentiate between gain and shape changes.

span.label: an alternative noise-aware shape-change method
span.quote: To confirm that these results were robust with respect to measurement noise, we also computed shape changes using an alternative method developed by ( David et al., 2008 ) (described in more detail in Methods and Supplementary Data ), and replicated the same trends discussed below.

span.label: Engaging in the detection task reduced overall STRF gain in the majority of recorded cells relative to the passive state.
span.quote: Compared to responses in the passive state, STRF gain decreased during task performance in most cells.

span.label: Shape changes, unlike gain changes, were excitatory and frequency-specific, concentrated in cells tuned near the target tone.
span.quote: By contrast, STRF shape changes were excitatory and specific, being strongest in cells with best frequencies near the target tone.

span.label: The combined gain and shape adaptations sharpened the target-versus-noise representation differently at high and low SNR.
span.quote: The net effect of these adaptations was to accentuate the representation of the target tone relative to the noise, by enhancing responses of near -target cells to the tone during high-SNR tasks, while suppressing responses of far -from-target cells to the masking noise in low-SNR tasks.

span.label: The magnitude of receptive-field adaptation tracked behavioural performance, being greatest in the best-performing sessions.
span.quote: These adaptive STRF changes were largest in high-performance sessions, confirming a close correlation with behavior

span.label: Suppression of receptive fields grew as the task became harder and reached significance only in the low-SNR condition.
span.quote: Suppression was weak in high and mid SNR tasks, and became significant (mean = −13.1 %; p < 0.05) only in the low SNR tasks.

span.label: Behaviourally, lick withdrawal time lengthened as target SNR fell, in all three ferrets.
span.quote: However, when TORCs were added to the target and SNR decreased, ferrets’ LWT increased, as shown in Fig.2B , for all three animals tested.

span.label: Identical intermediate-difficulty probe trials were detected better inside difficult blocks than inside easy blocks, indicating higher attentional engagement during hard tasks.
span.quote: Specifically, average discrimination-rate during hard blocks was 52.6% compared to 69.2% for the probe trials, whereas during easy blocks, average discrimination-rate was 72.9% during easy blocks compared to 58.6% on the probe trials.

span.label: Naive animals exposed to the identical stimuli showed no consistent receptive-field changes, so behaviour is required for the plasticity.
span.quote: We observed some minor, but no consistent changes in the STRFs in the absence of behavior, as illustrated in Figure SD-2 in Supplementary Data .

span.label: The gain reduction was a broad, difficulty-independent effect present in near and far cells alike, in contrast to the difficulty-dependent shape changes.
span.quote: This change was the same regardless of task difficulty, and occurred across most cells (near or far).

span.label: Going from high to low SNR targets suppressed firing to the reference noise by roughly a third.
span.quote: Furthermore, increasing task difficulty from high to low SNR targets caused a uniform overall suppression of about one third in the firing rate (as indicated by the dashed lines of Fig.7A ).

span.label: gain decreased in most cells during task performance while shape changes were excitatory and specific
span.quote: Compared to responses in the passive state, STRF gain decreased during task performance in most cells. By contrast, STRF shape changes were excitatory and specific, being strongest in cells with best frequencies near the target tone.

span.label: near-target cells were enhanced and far-from-target cells suppressed, within every difficulty level
span.quote: However, when we grouped the plasticity changes by near and far cells, it became apparent that near cells on average were enhanced (red) whereas far cells were suppressed (blue).

span.label: suppression became significant only in the low SNR tasks, at about -13%
span.quote: Suppression was weak in high and mid SNR tasks, and became significant (mean = −13.1 %; p < 0.05) only in the low SNR tasks.

span.label: the same tone placed far from a cell's BF produced suppression where near placement produced enhancement
span.quote: However, in sharp contrast, when the tone was placed far from a unit’s BF, the STRF change became suppressive in high SNR tasks.

span.label: changes were larger in the best-performing third of sessions
span.quote: The trend of increasing suppression for low SNRs (e.g., as in Fig.5 ) is repeated here, but with an important difference: STRF changes were amplified.

span.label: naive animals given identical stimuli showed no consistent STRF changes
span.quote: To demonstrate further the crucial role of behavior in inducing these changes, we measured STRF changes in 93 units from 3 naïve animals using exactly the same stimuli and analysis procedures as those used in the behavioral animals. We observed some minor, but no consistent changes in the STRFs in the absence of behavior, as illustrated in Figure SD-2 in Supplementary Data .

span.label: raising difficulty suppressed firing to the reference noise by about a third overall
span.quote: Furthermore, increasing task difficulty from high to low SNR targets caused a uniform overall suppression of about one third in the firing rate (as indicated by the dashed lines of Fig.7A ).

span.label: probe trials of identical difficulty were detected about 10% better inside hard blocks than inside easy ones
span.quote: Thus, performance on the probe trials (for the same SNR level intermediate probes) varied ~10% depending on overall block difficulty or attentional load (from 58.6% to 69.2%).

span.label: gain was at or below 1 in most cells, with medians near 0.9 for near-high-SNR and 0.7 for far-low-SNR
span.quote: In a majority of cells (> 66% in high SNR and near STRFs, and >80% in low SNR and far cells), the gain was <= 1 (median of approximately 0.9 and 0.7, respectively) indicating an overall suppression of the gain during behavior.

span.quote: To explore how performance correlated with STRF changes, we ranked the performance level for all experiments (as defined by the discrimination rate for behavioral sessions in individual physiology experiments; see Methods ) and then computed the average difference between active and passive STRFs for the experiments with best (top third) behavioral performance.

span.label: 237 — single cells in the population analysis of receptive-field plasticity, from two behaving ferrets
span.quote: To obtain a global view of the receptive field plasticity in these tasks, and the factors that influenced the nature of this plasticity, we examined STRF changes in a population of 237 cells from two animals.

span.label: 93, 57, and 87 — single units in the high, mid and low SNR difficulty groups respectively
span.quote: The three non-overlapping ranges were: high SNR (>=0 dB), mid SNR (0 dB > SNR >= −5 dB), low SNR (< −5 dB), with 93, 57, and 87 single-units in each range, respectively.

span.quote: Suppression was weak in high and mid SNR tasks, and became significant (mean = −13.1 %; p < 0.05) only in the low SNR tasks.

span.label: 10–30% — reduction in STRF gain caused by task engagement
span.quote: By assuming that STRF changes were the superposition of a global gain change and an orthogonal shape change, the analysis revealed that engagement in the tasks resulted in a substantial (10–30%) reduction in STRF gain during behavior ( Fig.7B ). This change was the same regardless of task difficulty, and occurred across most cells (near or far).

span.quote: In a majority of cells (> 66% in high SNR and near STRFs, and >80% in low SNR and far cells), the gain was <= 1 (median of approximately 0.9 and 0.7, respectively) indicating an overall suppression of the gain during behavior.

span.label: 58.6% versus 69.2% — probe detection in easy versus hard blocks at identical SNR
span.quote: Thus, performance on the probe trials (for the same SNR level intermediate probes) varied ~10% depending on overall block difficulty or attentional load (from 58.6% to 69.2%).

span.label: 93 units from 3 naive animals — the no-behaviour control
span.quote: To demonstrate further the crucial role of behavior in inducing these changes, we measured STRF changes in 93 units from 3 naïve animals using exactly the same stimuli and analysis procedures as those used in the behavioral animals. We observed some minor, but no consistent changes in the STRFs in the absence of behavior, as illustrated in Figure SD-2 in Supplementary Data .

span.label: 350 ms — lick withdrawal time for a pure-tone target
span.quote: In order to develop a quantitative behavioral index of task difficulty, we measured the average lick withdrawal time (LWT) of the animal, which we defined to be the time after target onset when the animal to decreased its lick rate to half its average lick rate during the reference stimuli (i.e., down to 40% from 80% in Figure 2A ).
